headline: No albies yet at Great Point — but the bluefish are pinning bait against every rip on the Shoals
subhead: Terns are diving, blues are blitzing, bass have gone to the dark hours — and the first bonito push is still a few tide cycles away.
body_markdown:
I sat off the tip of Great Point Wednesday morning with the engine idling, watching a mixed flock of terns and a couple gulls working a nervous patch of water maybe eighty yards off the rip line. Bait was getting pushed up tight — sand eels, some peanut bunker mixed in — and every few seconds something would explode underneath it, white water and all. I'll be honest, my first thought was albie. Second look, watching the boils roll instead of blow straight up, told me different. Bluefish. Good ones, three to six pounds, just wrecking that bait ball on the last of the ebb.

That's been the story all week from Great Point down through Sankaty and out onto the Shoals — bluefish are the show right now, and they're not shy about it. The water's sitting warm, mid-to-upper 70s in the shallows on a calm afternoon, and that heat has pushed the striped bass into their summer pattern — deep, structure-oriented, mostly nocturnal. Bluefish don't care. They're riding the same bait schools that have been pouring through the Sound for weeks, and they'll hit it in bright sun same as dusk.

Best tactic right now is metal — half-ounce to two-ounce diamond jigs snapped hard on the retrieve, or a bomber-style popper walked across the top when they're up busting bait visibly. Great Point rip on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most reliable window, but I've had similar action off Monomoy Rip and along the edge of Horseshoe Shoal where the current stacks bait against the drop. Don't overthink the retrieve — blues want speed and flash, not finesse. A few guys working topwater poppers off Sankaty at first light have had some of the better blitz sessions of the summer, fish crashing the surface so hard you can hear it from fifty yards.

Striped bass are around, just not where you'll find them at noon. The pattern's been consistent — fish holding deep on the current seams and ledges through the day, then sliding up onto structure after dark to feed. Chatham's inlet structure and the deeper cuts around Monomoy have been producing after-dark bass on chunked bunker and live eels, fished on the bottom or drifted just off it where the current runs hardest. If you want a shot at a real fish, that's the window — an hour before to an hour after the tide turns, dark water, patience. Daytime bass bites have been the exception, not the rule, and I wouldn't plan a whole trip around one.

Fluke have softened up in the shallower stuff as the heat's pushed them toward deeper water. The better fish have been coming from the channel edges and rip-adjacent structure around Monomoy and the deeper cuts off the Sound side of Nantucket — 25 to 40 feet, moving water, white or chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along bottom. It's not a numbers game right now, more a quality-over-quantity deal, but there are keepers mixed in if you're willing to work the drift instead of anchoring up and waiting.

Now — the question everyone's been asking me at the dock for two weeks straight. No, I have not seen a confirmed bonito or albie on Nantucket Shoals yet. I've been watching Great Point and the rips off Sankaty every day this week for that telltale sign — smaller, tighter boils, fish that come up and vanish instead of thrashing on top — and it just hasn't shown. Water off Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard has already crossed the temperature threshold that usually kicks this fishery off, and the moon's building toward full in early August, which means current through these rips is only going to get stronger over the next several days. Nantucket typically lags that Vineyard/Buzzards push by a week or two most years, and I don't see any reason this season breaks that pattern. If I had to guess, I'd say we're close — close enough that I'll have my epoxy jigs and Albie Snax rigged and ready every time I leave the dock.

We said last week this zone would hold steady with no major shifts coming, and that's exactly what's played out — the bluefish blitz has kept rolling, the bass have stayed nocturnal, and nothing's changed in a hurry. That stability actually works in our favor here, because it means when the current does build enough to pull bonito and albies up over the Shoals, the bait and the structure will be sitting exactly where we expect them.

For the coming week, I'd focus mornings and evenings on Great Point and Monomoy Rip for bluefish on metal and poppers, keep a bunker chunk or eel rig ready after dark around Chatham and Monomoue's deeper structure for bass, and check the Great Point rip line every single day for that first small, tight boil that doesn't look like a bluefish. If the building current does its job over the next few tide cycles, that's when this whole report changes.
